segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: A list is a collection of items with a single item written on each line.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: And they're everywhere. Shopping lists, to-do lists, even bucket lists.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: A list of all the things a person would like to do before they die.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: In fact, there's an episode of 6 Minute English all about them.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Imagine you're at the supermarket and find someone's shopping list.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: This happens a lot to Jo Nolan, a linguistics researcher whose new book explores our love of lists.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Here's Jo reading her shopping list on BBC Radio 4 programme Word of Mouth.

segments.speaker: Jo Nolan
segments.text: I only list the first four items, but the list read

segments.speaker: Jo Nolan
segments.text: Nana's, Ai Ai, Puke, Shrooms

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Nana's, Ai Ai, Puke, Shrooms?

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Can you work out what Joe was buying at the supermarket, Phil?

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: OK, well, I'm going to guess that Nana's are bananas and shrooms.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: They've got to be mushrooms, right?

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: OK, but what about Ai Ai and Puke?

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: what could they mean? Well, here's Jo's explanation to Michael Rosen, presenter of BBC Radio 4's

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Word of Mouth And let just come back to puke I mean were you instructing yourself to be sick in the supermarket I just a bit lost there

segments.speaker: Jo Nolan
segments.text: No it slightly grotesque My husband doesn like cucumber and the abbreviation for cucumber would be cuke

segments.speaker: Jo Nolan
segments.text: So he has always referred to it as puke.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: Aha! Cucumbers make Joanna's husband puke, a slang word for vomit.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: And puke rhymes with cuke.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: So it's a way of reminding her to buy cucumbers.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: Wow, sometimes lists are like secret codes.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: In this episode, we'll find out why people love lists and learn some useful new words and phrases.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: And remember, you'll find another list of all the vocabulary used on our website, bbclearningenglish.com.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: But first, a question for you, Beth.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: According to the list on the Internet Movie Database website, which movie has made the most money ever?

segments.text: Is it A. Titanic

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: B. Avengers Endgame

segments.speaker: Phil

segments.text: I think it might be Avatar

segments.text: although that might have been the most expensive to make.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: I'm not sure.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: OK, well we'll find out at the end of the programme.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: Popular songs are full of lists

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: and one of the most famous is My Favourite Things

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: sung by Julie Andrews in the film The Sound of Music.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: The song lists all her favourite things, from raindrops on roses to whiskers on kittens.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: Here Jo Nolan and Michael Rosen discuss the song on BBC Radio 4 programme Word of Mouth

segments.speaker: Jo Nolan
segments.text: I feel like you get a big bang for your buck in that song

segments.speaker: Jo Nolan
segments.text: Maybe it's the positivity. It's a bit saccharine. Maybe that's also part of the issue.

segments.speaker: Jo Nolan
segments.text: The list encourages you to think really efficiently and economically.

segments.speaker: Jo Nolan
segments.text: So I think you don't waste a lot of time and effort making a nice sentence or using long words.

segments.speaker: Jo Nolan
segments.text: You just get to the nub of things quite quickly.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: The song's list of favourite things is long,

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: and Jo says you get a big bang for your buck,

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: an idiom meaning that you gain a lot in return for the money or effort you spend on something.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: But not everyone likes the song.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Some call it saccharine, an adjective meaning excessively sweet, sentimental or insincere.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: Lists often abbreviate the items they contain.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: so you get to the nub of things quickly.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: The nub of something means the most important or essential point about it.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Lists can be useful as well.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Here's Jo Nolan giving an example of a useful list to BBC Radio 4's Word of Mouth.

segments.speaker: Jo Nolan
segments.text: A friend of mine who makes pros and cons lists

segments.speaker: Jo Nolan
segments.text: finds that it really helps her resolve a situation.

segments.speaker: Jo Nolan
segments.text: She halves her page, pros, cons, and she said by the end of it she knows what she's doing.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: Lists help us make decisions by writing down all the pros and cons of a situation.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: The pros and cons is another way of saying the advantages and disadvantages of something especially when you trying to choose between them

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: The more you think about it the more you see lists everywhere in menus and bank statements

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: for example. And therapists even recommend listing all the good things in your life

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: to feel happier. Not bad for a few words on a scrap of paper.

segments.text: OK, it's time to reveal the answer to my question.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: Beth, I asked you which movie had made the most money ever and you said Avatar.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: And now, according to the Internet Movie Database, that's exactly right.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Yay!

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: OK, let's recap the vocabulary we've learned, starting with bucket list.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: All the things you would like to do before you die.

segments.speaker: Beth

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: If something gives bang for your buck, you gain a lot of extra value in return for the money or effort you put into it.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: If you call something saccharine, you criticise it for being too sweet or sentimental.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: The nub of a problem or situation is the most important or essential thing about it.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: And finally, something's pros and cons are its advantages and disadvantages.
